task.goal: Keep a neighborhood mutual-aid pantry stocked without making donations unpredictable for recipients.
hard_constraints: Three volunteers, one shelf and a weekly inventory count; no cash collection.
Do not display recipient names or reserve food by perceived deservingness.
Track stockouts, spoilage, volunteer time and unmet requests.
task.available_resources: Paper tally and existing donation schedule.
task.expected_result: A workable allocation and replenishment routine.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Recurring staple commitments
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make replenishment more predictable by asking existing donors to commit to specific staple categories on their existing donation dates. Commitments are voluntary gifts of food, never money. This changes the supply mechanism: donors fill recurring gaps instead of independently guessing what to bring.

At the weekly inventory count, one volunteer records usable quantities, spoilage and anonymous unmet requests by category. The three volunteers select a short core list based on observed requests and suitable shelf-stable foods. Set modest weekly targets that fit the single shelf; treat these as planning targets, not guaranteed availability. Ask scheduled donors to choose a category and quantity they can repeat, and to report missed deliveries when possible. Unexpected donations remain welcome if safe and space permits. Publish the actual delivery schedule and clearly distinguish expected donations from food already available.

Use open access with a posted request to take a modest quantity of scarce staples per visit. Apply the same guidance to everyone, without names, eligibility judgments or individual reservations. Put earlier-expiring safe food at the front.

Divide responsibility among donor coordination, shelf care and weekly records, rotating roles if useful. On the paper tally, record each observed stockout and its discovery date, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests. An empty category found during the weekly count has an unknown stockout start time; do not imply continuous monitoring.

This requires enough repeat donors willing to make realistic commitments and a way to contact them already associated with the donation schedule. It cannot guarantee supply when commitments fail or demand rises. Start with only a few staples so coordination remains feasible.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use two existing weeks as a comparator, or record two baseline weeks if none exist, then try commitments for four weeks. Compare core-category stockouts and unmet requests alongside delivered quantities, spoilage and volunteer minutes. The mechanism is doubtful if commitments repeatedly go unfilled or gaps do not fall despite similar demand and donation volume. Treat a short trial as provisional evidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A visible buffer with scheduled releases
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Smooth access across the week by dividing suitable donations between immediate availability and a small, openly explained buffer released on fixed days. The mechanism changes when food becomes available, reducing the chance that a delivery is exhausted immediately and leaves later visitors with nothing.

At the weekly count, estimate the coming week's usable shelf-stable supply. Leave most available immediately and mark a small section of the same shelf as the next scheduled release, using paper labels. Choose release times the three volunteers can reliably cover, preferably during existing donation visits. Publish the times and explain that the buffer belongs to the whole community; nothing is assigned to named recipients. All visitors face the same release rules, and anyone may take food from the available section without a deservingness assessment.

Use the buffer only for durable, commonly requested items. Perishables and food nearing its safe-use limit go directly into circulation. If demand is low or a release would create spoilage, release the buffer early and note the exception. If the shelf cannot clearly distinguish available stock from the buffer, this approach is unsuitable. It also depends on visitors respecting the labels; volunteers should not police identities or maintain recipient lists.

One volunteer leads the weekly count, while the other two handle scheduled releases and shelf care. Record available-section stockouts separately from total depletion: food held for later does not make a present unmet request disappear. Tally spoilage, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests, including requests made while buffer stock remains. Log stockout discovery and refill dates without claiming exact durations.

No storage beyond the one shelf is needed. The main tradeoff is explicit: retaining food for later visitors may deny an immediate request. Keep the buffer small and change or abandon it if that tradeoff worsens access.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare two ordinary weeks with four buffer weeks, alternating approaches if practical. Track unmet requests and stockouts by early versus late week, plus total spoilage and volunteer time. The buffer fails if later access does not improve, total unmet requests increase, or releases are frequently missed. Compare donation quantities and visitor-request tallies before attributing changes to release timing.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Equal flexible shares across food categories
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Stretch scarce staples across more visits through a simple, universal share rule with recipient-chosen substitutions. The mechanism changes allocation: instead of unrestricted early depletion of a popular item, everyone is asked to take the same modest share while choosing among available alternatives.

During the weekly count, group suitable food into a few understandable categories, such as meal bases, proteins and vegetables. Keep foods in their original packaging on the single shelf; no bags or additional storage are required. Post a paper guide such as 'Please start with one item from each available category per visit.' Choose quantities from actual supply, and relax the guidance for abundant items or items nearing expiry. Explain that this is a shared starting allowance, not a nutritionally complete household ration.

Recipients choose their own items and may decline unsuitable food. Clearly labeled alternatives within a category can satisfy different preferences, but never assume they meet an allergy, religious or medical requirement. Record requests for unavailable suitable options as unmet even when other food remains. Do not require names, proof of need or staff judgments about who deserves more. Use a voluntary rule rather than recipient tracking; repeat visits and uneven household needs remain limitations.

Use the existing donation schedule to ask for whichever categories are repeatedly missing. One volunteer prepares the weekly category guidance, another checks safe stock rotation during existing visits, and the third maintains the tally; rotate these duties as desired. Record category and item stockouts, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests. Count an empty category as a gap even if the shelf still contains plenty of another category.

This needs understandable categories, enough variety to make choice meaningful and broad cooperation. It may distribute scarce food more widely, but cannot correct insufficient total supply and may be too restrictive for larger households.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare two weeks of the current access routine with four weeks of flexible shares. Examine scarce-item stockouts, anonymous unmet requests, spoilage and volunteer minutes alongside incoming quantities. Add an optional anonymous paper question: 'Could you take food you could use?' Reject or revise the routine if usable access declines, conflicts increase, or scarce items disappear just as quickly under comparable supply.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Spread donation arrivals across the week
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Reduce gaps by moving clustered donation visits to different days on the existing schedule. The mechanism is steadier incoming supply: food reaches the shelf several times during the week, giving later visitors access to fresh arrivals and reducing crowding that can cause spoilage. All delivered food becomes available immediately.

At the weekly inventory count, compare the existing donation schedule with paper records of empty categories and shelf overflow. Ask existing donors whether they can shift their usual delivery to an uncovered part of the week, without increasing their donation or promising particular items. Start by moving just one delivery. Publish agreed delivery windows as expected arrivals, clearly stating that contents and availability can vary. Record cancellations when known; never advertise an expected donation as food already available.

Keep allocation open and consistent: recipients choose from available food, with no names, individual reservations or judgments of deservingness. Place safe, earlier-expiring items at the front. Do not hold back food to make the schedule appear reliable.

One volunteer coordinates schedule changes, one maintains the shelf during already planned visits, and one leads the weekly inventory and tally. Record incoming quantities by broad category, observed stockouts and discovery dates, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests. Leave a paper space for visitors to mark missing items voluntarily. These reports are incomplete observations, not a count of everyone who went without.

This requires clustered arrivals, donors able to change delivery days, and deliveries that do not require extra volunteer trips. It uses the same shelf and paper records. If donations already arrive evenly, donors cannot shift visits, or total supply is inadequate, changing arrival times may offer little benefit.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Record two weeks under the current schedule, then try four weeks with one delivery shifted into a recurring gap. Keep ordinary allocation unchanged. Compare late-week observed stockouts and unmet requests, incoming quantities, spoilage and volunteer minutes. Also check whether gaps simply move earlier in the week. Reject the change if shifted deliveries are unreliable, require extra trips the volunteers cannot sustain, or show no improvement under roughly comparable supply and reported demand. Sparse reports and changing donation contents limit any conclusion.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Weekly gap slips: replenish what was used or requested
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a weekly feedback rule to direct existing donations toward current gaps. Instead of asking donors for standing staple commitments, give each scheduled donation a short, updated list of missing foods and maximum useful quantities. The mechanism is demand-responsive replenishment: scarce shelf space and donor effort follow actual use and unmet requests, while limits discourage repeated surpluses.

At the weekly count, record usable stock by a few food categories. On the same paper tally, record donations received and anonymous requests for unavailable foods. Estimate consumption from opening stock plus arrivals minus closing stock and recorded spoilage; acknowledge that unrecorded movements make this approximate. For each category, use the previous week's estimated consumption plus unmet requests as an initial weekly target. Subtract usable stock and cap the requested amount at the space available on the single shelf. Volunteers should review unusually large changes rather than automatically amplifying noisy tallies.

Assign each gap to one existing donation slot so multiple donors are not asked to fill the same shortage. Pass the list through the existing scheduling arrangement, or give donors paper slips during their visits for their next delivery. Donors remain free to decline; no purchases, money collection or extra trips are required. Make all safe delivered food immediately available, rotate earlier-expiring food forward, and use open recipient choice without names, reservations or deservingness judgments.

One volunteer counts and calculates gaps, one passes slips through the schedule, and one maintains the tally and shelf during existing visits. Record observed stockouts with discovery dates, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests. Post actual availability separately from requested donations.

This requires donors who can adjust donation contents and reasonably complete arrival records. Weekly feedback can lag sudden demand changes, and cannot overcome insufficient donations. Targets are planning estimates, not promises to recipients.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Record two weeks of ordinary donations, then use gap slips for three weeks. Compare category stockouts and unmet requests alongside incoming quantities, spoilage and volunteer minutes. Inspect whether requested gaps actually receive food and whether surplus categories shrink. Reject or simplify the routine if donors cannot respond before the next count, recordkeeping becomes burdensome, or shortages persist despite comparable total supply and demand. Sparse anonymous tallies limit conclusions.

EXPAND.title: Trigger replacement requests when a staple runs low
EXPAND.proposal:
Replace calendar-only replenishment with a small feedback loop: an observed low-stock condition triggers a specific food request to donors already on the donation schedule. Unlike recurring staple commitments, this responds to actual depletion rather than assuming the same weekly quantity will suffice.

At the weekly inventory, choose two frequently requested, shelf-stable categories. Give each a marked shelf space and a simple trigger, initially one remaining usable unit. Set a refill ceiling that fits its space. During visits volunteers already make, they inspect these categories; this adds no mandatory visits or extra full inventory counts. Recipients may also leave an anonymous low-stock mark on the paper tally, which a volunteer verifies before contacting donors.

Assign one volunteer to verify and record triggers, one to contact the next scheduled donor, and one to handle delivery and rotation. A request states the category, maximum quantity and next useful delivery date. Record whether a donor accepts; if declined or unanswered by the next existing volunteer visit, approach the following scheduled donor. Close the request when food arrives, preventing duplicate deliveries. All usable food remains available under the pantry's ordinary equal-access practice, without recipient names or individual reservations.

Use the tally for observed stockouts and discovery dates, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests. A threshold alert is not itself an unmet request. Post confirmed delivery dates separately from current availability; never promise a refill that nobody has accepted.

This requires an existing way to reach scheduled donors and donors able to adjust their gifts. Sparse volunteer visits or long delivery delays may make alerts too late. If those prerequisites are absent, this route is unsuitable.
EXPAND.experiment: The donor-contact volunteer owns a four-week trial covering two staples. Compare it with the same categories under recurring commitments, using existing records or two prospective comparator weeks. Compare observed stockouts and unmet requests alongside incoming quantities, spoilage and volunteer minutes; weekly observations cannot establish exact stockout durations. Stop early if duplicate requests exceed shelf capacity or coordination exceeds a pre-agreed 30 additional volunteer minutes per week. Reject the mechanism if gaps do not fall under reasonably comparable supply and demand, or if any improvement requires unsustainable extra work.

EXPAND.title: Prevent usable donations from becoming shelf losses
EXPAND.proposal:
Increase dependable supply by preventing avoidable spoilage and damaged or forgotten stock. The mechanism preserves food already donated; it does not depend on recruiting additional supply or dividing access into scheduled releases.

At the weekly count, one volunteer examines packaging, applicable storage requirements and dates using locally applicable food-safety guidance. Record usable quantities and spoiled units separately. Arrange each category so suitable items needing earlier use are easiest to reach. Keep original labels visible and leave every usable item available immediately. Use a paper shelf map to stop newer deliveries from hiding older food.

On the existing donation schedule, write the shelf's practical intake limits: foods that can safely remain on this shelf, intact packaging and quantities that fit without crushing or obscuring stock. A second volunteer communicates these limits to scheduled donors. When the shelf cannot safely accommodate a delivery, ask the donor to retain the excess and offer it on a later existing donation date; do not create an overflow store. This depends on donor cooperation and cannot be treated as confirmed future stock.

The third volunteer checks placement when receiving donations and records exceptions. If nobody can assess an item's safety, leave it with its donor pending clarification; do not place questionable food among available stock. No recipient names, eligibility judgments or personal reservations are used.

The weekly tally records observed stockouts, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests, including requests for suitable food when unusable stock occupies space. Also record quantities deferred or declined so reduced spoilage cannot disguise reduced supply.

Compared with recurring commitments, this route addresses loss after delivery. It is most promising when spoilage or poor placement is consequential; it will have little effect if nearly everything already leaves safely and promptly.
EXPAND.experiment: The inventory volunteer owns two baseline weeks followed by four weeks using the intake and rotation routine. Compare usable availability, observed stockouts and unmet requests with the ordinary recurring-donation routine, accounting for quantities received and deferred. Track spoilage and added volunteer minutes together. Stop if intake handling repeatedly delays recipients or leaves less usable food available because donors cannot retain excess. Keep the routine only if avoided losses improve access enough to justify the work; lower recorded spoilage alone is insufficient evidence.

EXPAND.title: Improvement to P0: Recurring staple commitments with a missed-delivery fallback
EXPAND.proposal:
Preserve P0’s mechanism: existing donors voluntarily repeat specific food contributions on their existing donation dates. Repair its main weakness by making a missed commitment change both replenishment action and public information. A commitment alone cannot prevent an empty shelf.

At the weekly count, select two frequently requested shelf-stable categories and targets that fit the single shelf. Ask scheduled donors what quantities they can realistically repeat; do not assign unsupported targets. On paper, distinguish food present, donor-confirmed deliveries and unconfirmed expectations. Publish dates as expected arrivals, without guaranteeing availability.

One volunteer coordinates donors. If a delivery is reported missed, or is absent when a volunteer next attends, that volunteer crosses out its expected arrival and asks the next already-scheduled donor whether they can supply the gap within the shelf’s capacity. Record acceptance before treating it as expected supply. Cancel the replacement request if the original donor subsequently delivers. This transfers some uncertainty into coordination work, so record that time, including unsuccessful contacts.

A second volunteer receives food and places earlier-use items first. The third owns the weekly count and tally. All usable food is immediately available, with the same voluntary modest-share guidance for everyone. No cash, recipient names, eligibility judgments or individual reservations are involved. Record observed stockouts and discovery dates, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests; weekly observations cannot establish exact stockout durations.

This requires existing donor contact access and some willingness to repeat gifts. If donors cannot commit or replacements repeatedly fail, revert to the existing donation schedule and publish only food actually present. Unlike P1, this does not withhold food from current visitors, but recipients still bear shortages when supply fails.
EXPAND.experiment: The tally owner runs four weeks against the preceding two weeks of ordinary scheduled donations, using the same recording method. Compare weekly observed staple gaps and unmet requests alongside spoilage, total volunteer minutes and failed replacement contacts; note donation quantities because supply changes confound attribution. Stop replacement chasing after one unsuccessful scheduled-donor contact per gap. Abandon commitments if shortages do not improve while coordination time rises. This trial can show no practical gain; it cannot establish reliable supply under unusual demand.

EXPAND.title: Improvement to P1: Scheduled releases only when a usable buffer exists
EXPAND.proposal:
Preserve P1’s mechanism of spreading availability through a small buffer on the same shelf, released at public, fixed times. Repair its execution weakness with an admission and recovery rule: buffering proceeds only when a volunteer can reliably release it and current access retains a modest supply. Otherwise every usable item stays available.

At the weekly count, choose at most one durable staple category. Buffer no more than one unit for every three units left immediately available, and only if the shelf can clearly separate the sections using paper labels. These are trial limits, not evidence of an optimal allocation. Name a release owner and a backup from the three volunteers, using visits they already make. If neither can cover a release, do not establish that buffer. Post release times and explain that held food is for general access, never named people.

At an existing volunteer visit, release the buffer early if the available portion is empty, a suitable request cannot be met while matching food is held, or continued holding risks spoilage. Record the exception. If no volunteer is present, the posted rule permits visitors to take held units when the available section is empty; cooperation is an assumption, not something enforced through identities. Recurring early release means this category is unsuitable for buffering.

One volunteer owns the count and allocation, another the release, and the third backup and records. Record available-section stockouts separately from total depletion, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests, including requests occurring while food is held. Unknown depletion times remain unknown.

Compared with P0, this can operate without donor commitments, but creates an immediate-access cost and cannot increase total supply. Keep every perishable or near-use-limit item available immediately. If labels cause confusion or recovery rules are impractical, remove the buffer and use ordinary open access.
EXPAND.experiment: The count owner alternates ordinary open access and buffering over four comparable weeks, retaining the existing donation schedule. At existing later-week visits, compare actual availability and anonymous unmet requests, while also comparing earlier unmet requests, spoilage and volunteer minutes. Record incoming quantities. Stop immediately after a missed release without backup, unsafe holding, or repeated confusion; stop after two buffering weeks if later availability shows no improvement or earlier unmet requests increase. Sparse observations may leave the result inconclusive.

EXPAND.title: Stagger donor arrivals to shorten replenishment gaps
EXPAND.proposal:
Change the timing of incoming donations, rather than securing recurring staple quantities or withholding food after arrival. Use the existing donation schedule to move one clustered delivery into a long uncovered interval. The mechanism is shorter gaps between replenishments, with every usable donation available immediately.

At the weekly count, mark the coming week’s scheduled deliveries on paper. Use previous stockout discoveries and anonymous unmet requests to identify a plausible gap; do not infer an exact depletion day from a weekly count. Ask one existing donor whether their normal delivery can move to that interval without an additional trip or unsafe food storage. Keep the quantity and food type unchanged for the first trial. This isolates timing as far as practical and avoids creating a new donor commitment programme.

One volunteer owns schedule changes and records both the original and accepted dates. A second receives food during an existing feasible volunteer visit and rotates earlier-use items forward. The third maintains the weekly tally. If a donor cannot shift, retain the original date. If a shifted delivery is cancelled, immediately remove its expected arrival from the public schedule and resume the donor’s original schedule for subsequent weeks. Do not promise an immediate replacement.

All food occupies the single shelf; no pantry buffer or overflow storage is created. Post current stock information separately from expected delivery dates. Use equal open access without recipient names, deservingness assessments or individual reservations. Record observed stockouts and discovery dates, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests.

This requires clustered arrivals, a donor with genuine timing flexibility and compatible receiving access. It has little value when donations already arrive evenly or total supply is inadequate. Unlike P1, it avoids holding pantry food back, but may transfer inconvenience or storage costs to donors. Accept only shifts they report as manageable; shelf-stable, intact food is the simplest starting point.
EXPAND.experiment: The schedule owner tests one delivery shift for two weeks, following two weeks on the existing schedule with identical tallying. Compare observed gaps and unmet requests, incoming quantities, spoilage and volunteer minutes; ask the participating donor whether the shift added travel or storage difficulty. Stop and restore the original date if a shift causes a missed delivery, unsafe storage or an extra trip. Retain it only if access appears better without increased donor or volunteer burden; unchanged gaps would falsify its practical value locally.
